Bring the tunnel back up if it drops unexpectedly. Retries once per drop.
When the tunnel drops, reconnect through the next-best node instead of the one that just failed. Groups already pick for themselves, so this only applies to a single node.
Send individual apps direct, or through a specific node.
Each app can follow the tunnel, leave the device directly, or use a specific node. This is applied when the tunnel is built, so it takes effect from the next connection.
Nodes, groups and rules in one encrypted file. It is useless without the passphrase — there is no recovery.
scrypt + AES-256-GCM. The passphrase is never stored.
Wrong passphrase, or the file is damaged.
Starveil runs on this device. This page lists everything that leaves it, and there is nothing you did not ask it to send.

Nothing. No account, no analytics, no advertising identifier, and no crash reporting in this version. The project runs no server of its own, so there is nowhere for data to be sent even if it were collected.
Nodes, groups, routing rules, logs and latency history live in a SQLCipher-encrypted database in the app’s private storage. The database key is held in the Android keystore.

Two kinds of address only: the nodes and subscription URLs you imported, and — when the mainland preset is on — the rule-set files it downloads from jsDelivr or GitHub. Those requests reach a public CDN, not the author.
VPN, to route traffic. Notifications, for the ongoing tunnel notice. The installed-app list is read only to draw the per-app routing screen, and it never leaves the device.

A backup is written wherever you choose, encrypted with scrypt and AES-256-GCM. The passphrase is never stored, and it cannot be recovered — without it the file is useless to everyone, including the author.
Uninstalling removes the database and the keystore entries with it. Backup files are yours to keep or delete.
